title: Instruments in the room
hookLine: harmonium and tabla today, and older strings like the rebab and saranda

lines: A BOX, A BELLOWS, TWO DRUMS.
cards: During kirtan in a gurdwara, look toward the front, near the Guru Granth Sahib. Often a few musicians sit on a low platform.
One or two have a small wooden box in front of them, pumping a bellows at the back with one hand and pressing keys with the other. Another sits behind a pair of drums, fingers flickering.
It all looks ancient and timeless. But in Guru Nanak's gatherings, as Sikhs tell it, none of those instruments were there. There was a man with a stringed instrument across his lap.
The sounds in the room have changed. What they're for hasn't.

teach.b: Start with the box. That's the harmonium, a small reed organ; Punjabis often just call it the vaaja.
It came to India with Europeans in the nineteenth century, and a hand-pumped version made for sitting on the floor caught on fast. Today it's at the heart of gurdwara kirtan.

Beside it, the tabla, a pair of hand drums, keeps the rhythm and the pulse. Now go back further. Guru Nanak's companion Mardana, whom you met on day thirty-one, played the rebab, a plucked string instrument.
Tradition links other strings to later Gurus: the saranda, a bowed instrument, to Guru Arjan; the taus, shaped like a peacock, to Guru Hargobind; the dilruba to Guru Gobind Singh.
Before the tabla, the older drum was the jori, a pair played with the hands.
In recent years, Sikh musicians and schools have been bringing the strings back. Some say the harmonium's fixed notes can't bend the way a raag wants to, and the old strings suit gurbani better.

Others love the harmonium: it's easy to learn, it carries a congregation well, and it's how their grandparents sang. Both are heard in gurdwaras today, often side by side. What doesn't change: no instrument is the point.
The Word is at the center, and every sound in the room is there to carry it. The drum holds the time. The strings or the reeds hold the melody.
And the sangat holds the listening.

how: Gurdwara kirtan today is often sung with harmonium and tabla, while a growing number of musicians and schools also teach the older string instruments, such as the rebab, saranda, taus and dilruba.

o: the everyday Punjabi name for the harmonium
a pair of hand drums that keeps the rhythm
a bowed string instrument from the Gurus' time

games.q: what's inside the room — tap the pairs.

s: the harmonium was played in Guru Nanak's time
it came to India with Europeans in the nineteenth century. Mardana played the rebab.
many Sikh musicians are bringing back the old string instruments
the saranda, taus, dilruba and rebab are being taught again.
Sikhs all agree the harmonium should be replaced
some prefer the strings for raag; others love the harmonium. both are heard today.

games.q: you're joining a kirtan group. one musician says only the old strings suit gurbani; another says the harmonium carries the congregation best. what will you hear in gurdwaras today?
o: use both, often side by side.
games.why: both are heard in gurdwaras today. what doesn't change is that every instrument is there to carry the Word.

practice: Play kirtan if you can, or any music with a few instruments; if there's none near you, use the sounds of the room. Follow only the drum, then only the melody, the harmonium or the strings, then only the voice.
Finally, let them all come back together, and hear how each one leans on the others.

wordCard.voice: Vaaja. The everyday Punjabi name for the harmonium, now at the heart of gurdwara kirtan alongside the tabla, and the rebab, saranda and taus of the Gurus' time.

carryVoice: Your line: every sound has a part. Harmonium or strings, the Word stays at the center. See you tomorrow.
